8/11/2023 - Concept: **Bange, M. P., & Milroy, S. P. (2004). Growth and dry matter partitioning of diverse cotton genotypes. Field Crops Research, 87(1), 73-87. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.fcr.2003.09.007**

Add (water)stress effect in cases where severe water deficit cutout reached earlier. See Hearn, 1969 paper where when 2/3 water supply depleted --> node production halts and plant shifts into cutout.

From PhD Warren Conaty:

Water stress also alters the time taken for a boll to reach maturity. Water deficits result in the hastening of maturity, whilst excessive soil water tends to slow maturity (Hearn, 1994; Hearn, 1979; Marani and Amirav, 1971b; Marani and Amirav, 1971a). This occurs as a result of the inherent plant water relations fixed within commercial cotton cultivars derived from its wild xerophytic ancestors. As a result, when two thirds of the soil water is used, vegetative growth ceases, boll setting and square production cease and the retained bolls mature. Boll setting and square production can resume, if conditions are favourable, when mature bolls open, leading to a second fruiting flush (Hearn, 1979).

To implement this stage, two moving averages of the Above Ground Wt are used as a multipler. The short average (3 Days) over the long average (21 days). When the plant is growing quickly, the averages will diverge and the modifier goes up, and when the growth slows, the long average catches up reducing the modifier.

This modifier is passed through a curve where when growth is low the phenology slows down (such in a slow growing environment), goes up to normal progression when growing at an average speed, then slows drastically if the boll growth is very high. This allows the larger yield areas that put on biomass faster to extend their cutout to maturity phase, while also allowing the slower growing areas to do the same.

This curve has been hand built based on the validation set, but could be replaced with a curve function at some point in the function to generalise it.

**Canopy Development**

Leaf area development is calculated as the net effect of leaf growth and senescence, removal of leaf by animals of management, and changes in specific leaf area of previous growth.  


Calculations are as follows:
 
```

Area  = InitialArea + AccumulatedChange
InitialArea = AreaPerPlant x Population
AccumulatedChange = AreaGrowth - AreaSenesced - AreaRemoved
If current growth stage is between emergence and maturity
   AreaGrowth = AreaGrowth + SpecificLeafArea x Allocated.StructuralWt
If current growth stage is between emergence and HarvestRipe
   AreaSenesced = AreaSenesced + SpecificLeafAreaCanopy x Senesced.StructuralWt
If current growth stage is between emergence and HarvestRipe
   AreaRemoved = AreaRemoved + SpecificLeafAreaCanopy x Removed.StructuralWt


```
 
where
 
Name | Description | Units
-|-|-
Area | Green leaf area per unit ground area | m^2^/m^2^
InitialArea | Leaf area of an individual plant at emerence | m^2^
AreaGrowth | Accumulated leaf area growth from emergence to maturity | m^2^/m^2^
AreaSenesced | Accumulated leaf area senescence from emergence to harvest ripe | m^2^/m^2^
AreaRemoved | Accumulated leaf area removed (e.g. grazing) from emergence to harvest ripe| m^2^/m^2^
SpecificLeafArea | Area per unit mass of green leaf for today's leaf growth | m^2^/g
SpecificLeafAreaCanopy | Area per unit mass of green leaf currently in the entire crop canopy | m^2^/g
Allocated.StructuralWt | Mass of dm allocated to the leaf from daily growth by the organ arbitrator. | g/m^2^
Senesced.StructuralWt | Mass of live dm senesced on the current day. | g/m^2^
Removed.StructuralWt | Mass of live dm removed on the current day. | g/m^2^
ThermalTime | Daily thermal time calculated by the phenology model | ^o^C


**Potential Leaf Growth**

Potential growth in leaf area is used to calculate the leaf dry matter demand.  The potential increase in leaf area is calculated with estimates of leaf appearance, branching dynamics and plant population.  The appearance and sizes of leaves are calculated for main stem leaves and sympodial leaves.  

Note that leaf biomass is assumed to consist of entirely structural dry matter.

Calculations are as follows:

```

DMDemand.Structural.Wt = deltaLAIPotential x SpecificLeafArea
DMDemand.Storage.Wt = 0.0
DMDemand.Metabolic.Wt = 0.0
DeltaLAIPotential = AreaLargestLeaf x RelativeArea x Population x StemNumberPerPlant x LAR x ExpansionStressFactor
LAR = ThermalTime / Phyllochron


```

where
 
Name | Description | Units
-|-|-
DMDemand.Structural.Wt | Daily potential leaf structural growth (ie daily DMD demand for leaf growth) | g/m<sup>2</sup>
deltaLAIPotential | Daily potential increase in LAI if DM supply from arbitrator is adequate | m<sup>2</sup>/m<sup>2</sup>/d
AreaLargestLeaf | The area of the largest leaf on the main stem. | m<sup>2</sup>
RelativeArea | The size of the currently expanding leaf compared to the largest leaf on the main stem | 0-1
StemNumberPerPlant | The number of currently expanding stems on each plant. | /plant
LAR | The Leaf Appearance Rate, or the number of leaves appearing on the current day. | /day
ThermalTime | Daily thermal time calculated by the phenology model | <sup>o</sup>C
Phyllochron | The thermal time required for the appearance of each leaf on the main stem. | <sup>o</sup>C


**Branching Dynamics**

The number of stems on each plant is calculated as an accumulation of fruiting and vegetative branches.  

Calculations are as follows:

```
BranchNumberPerPlant = FruitingBranchNumber + VegetativeBranchNumber

FruitingBranchNumber = 2 + number of nodes grown from squaring to cutout
VegetativeBranchNumber = 0

```

where
 
Name | Description | Units
-|-|-
BranchNumberPerPlant | Total number of branches on each plant | /plant
FruitingBranchNumber | Number of branches on each plant that will initiate a boll. | /plant
VegetativeBranchNumber | Number of branches on each plant that will NOT initiate a boll. | /plant


**Specific Green Leaf Area**

The cotton model estimates the specific leaf area of daily leaf growth directly rather than as an emergent property of separate area and mass growth functions as used in many earlier APSIM models.  Specific Leaf Area is a function of ambiant light conditions (ie via an estimate of daily Photosynthetically Active Radiation) which is then discounted by water stress or air temperature.

```
SpecificLeafArea = PotentialSpecificLeafArea x min (SWFactor, TemperatureFactor)

{[Cotton].Leaf.SpecificArea.Stage2.HoldFunction.SLA.PotentialSpecificLeafArea}

```

where
 
Name | Description | Units
-|-|-
SpecificLeafArea | Area per unit mass of green leaf for today's leaf growth | m<sup>2</sup>/g
PotentialSpecificLeafArea | SpecificLeafArea for daily leaf growth under current light conditions | m<sup>2</sup>/g
SLAmax | Specific Leaf Area under high light conditions| m<sup>2</sup>/g
SLAmax | Specific Leaf Area under low light conditions| m<sup>2</sup>/g
SLApar | Parameter describing the shape of the response of SLA to incoming PAR | unitless
SWFactor | Water Factor to reduce SpecificLeafArea under water limiting conditions </br> {[Cotton].Leaf.SpecificArea.Stage2.HoldFunction.SLA.SWFactor} </br> {[Cotton].Leaf.SpecificArea.Stage2.HoldFunction.SLA.SWFactor.TURSLA} | 0-1
TemperatureFactor | Temperature Factor to reduce SpecificLeafArea under low temperature conditions | 0-1


**Canopy Light Extinction Coefficients**

Canopy light interception is calculated by the methods described above (see light interception section in this chapter) using light extinction coefficients.  The extinction coefficient for green leaf is assumed to change with row spacing.  

{[Cotton].Leaf.ExtinctionCoefficient}

FROM:

Chapter 22. CottonJ. Snider, M. Bange and J. HeitholtIn: Crop Physiology. Case Histories for Major Crops, edited by V. O. Sadras and D. F. Calderini2021

"To encapsulate effects of changes in canopy radiation interception and/or changes in canopy photosynthesis, physiological frameworks have been developed to scale from leaf to canopy (Sinclair and Horie, 1989; Hammer and Wright 1994). With this framework, Sadras (1996) explained ontogenetic changes in cotton RUE, and Milroy and Bange (2003) explored the effects of average canopy specific leaf nitrogen (SLN g N m− 2), vertical N gradients (SLNgrad), extinction coefficient k and LAI. Sensitivity analyses indicated that RUE is responsive to SLNgrad and to a lesser extent, k (Fig. 22.7). Although the importance of these traits has been demonstrated in other crops, it has also been shown that they are of most significance at high LAI (Hirose and Werger, 1987). When the impact of SLNgrad on RUE was tested at different LAI, no impact was evident at low LAI, but a large impact was evident at LAI of 5. Although LAI of this magnitude can occur in cotton crops, lower LAI are more common with critical LAI being approximately 3 (Section 2.1.2). Thus the central finding is that there appears to be little impact of the ontogenetic changes in k and SLNgrad on the variation in RUE of cotton. For crop simulation purposes, this simplifies the process of adjusting RUE."

See also:

Nitrogen and Light Responses of Cotton Photosynthesis and Implications for Crop GrowthS. P. Milroy and M. P. BangeCrop Science 2003 Vol. 43 Pages 904-913

Children.Text:
The mainstem was therefore a simple parameter for the effect of age, temperature and water on the development of plant structure. 

The relationship was explained by a model in which fruiting branches compete with one another. The structure of the crop plants, as measured by the types and number of nodes, developed along a course in time determined by variety and spacing at a rate dependent on temperature. 

The rate decreased with age, but was **independent of the quantity of water available**, **until a critical amount had been used, when development stopped abruptly.**

**--> USE ASPF FACTOR to stop node production?!?!?**

From PhD Warren Conaty:

The relationship between morphogenesis and water supply in cotton is that once the cropgerminates, **morphogenesis is unaffected by water supply until approximately two-thirds of available water has been depleted**. At this point, the production of squares ceases, and if water supply is not replenished crop growth terminates and the set fruit is matured (Hearn and Constable, 1984).



========================

* Use separate thermal time in phenology for phyllochron?
* fruitload slows down node-development and halts at cutout

========================

FROM: *Hearn, A.B., 1994. The principles of cotton water relations and their application in management. In: G.A. Constable and N.W. Forrester (Editors), Challenging the Future: Proceedings of the World Cotton Research Conference. CSIRO, Brisbane, Australia, pp. 66–92.*

The plants with different amounts of stored water
develop at the same rate unaffected by the amount of water,
until approximately three quarters is exhausted, whereupon
morphological development and vegetative growth stop
abruptly. Consequently, the final size and shape of the plants
grown with different amounts of stored water look like
successive stages of one crop, which in effect is what they are.
This pattern of development is well adapted for survival in
arid' and semi-arid environments where the water supply
from rainfall or floods is erratic and variable. It allows the
plant to make full use of supplies which can va1y greatly from
one event or season to the next. When the supply is large,
development continues for longer to give a larger plant and
heavier yield, when the supply is !imaU the reverse occurs.
The key is that the plant somehow recognises that the water
supply is running out (the dry 'signal' in Fig. 2), and in
response stops further morphological development and
concentrates on maturing the fruit already set.

Each day's increment of leaf area is accounted for separately in order 
to facilitate senescence of leaves. Data on leaf longevity are sparse and 
variable; values range from 55 to 99 days and 500 to 1300 DD. Water 
stress early can delay development and lengthen life, while late in life it 
can accelerate senescence. Senescence appears to be accelerated when the 
crop has a full boll load, probably reflecting faster remobilisation of 
nitrogen. On the basis of Hesketh et al. (1977) and McMichael and 
Hesketh (1982) the day degree requirement for leaf senescence, SENLF, 
has been set to vary between 833 and 1100 as a function of SMI and 
fruit load thus: 
SENLF = 833 + 277*FB*FW 
where FW decreases linearly from l ·O when SMI = 0·25 to O·O when 
SMI = O·O, and FB in defined by 1 - LOAD/CARCAP, LOAD and 
CARCAP being defined previously. A day's leaves are senesced when the 
appropriate day degree requirement has been met.

Children.Text:
**Bur Dry Matter Demands**

Demands for DM growth is only for structural growth (ie no storage or metabolic demand).

```
{[Cotton].Bur.DMDemands.Structural.DMDemandFunction}
```

where

```
{[Cotton].Bur.DMDemands.Structural.DMDemandFunction.BurDevelopment.HIDemand.HarvestIndexIncrease}
OutstandingHarvestIndexIncrease = Max (0,Increase)
{[Cotton].Bur.DMDemands.Structural.DMDemandFunction.BurDevelopment.HIDemand.HarvestIndexIncrease.OutstandingHarvestIndexIncrease.Increase}
{[Cotton].Bur.DMDemands.Structural.DMDemandFunction.BurDevelopment.HIDemand.HarvestIndexIncrease.TTRemaining}
{[Cotton].Bur.PotentialHarvestIndex}
```

**Bur Nitrogen Demand and Allocation**

Bur Nitrogen allocation to structural, storage and metabolic biomass pools is calculated by the OrganArbitrator as described above.  The bur model calculates the demands for each of these pools from information on the minimum, critical and maximum bur Nitrogen concentration for each predicted stage of development.

The minimum bur nitrogen concentration is used to describe the nitrogen content of the structural bur material. The difference between minimum and critical nitrogen concentration is assumed to correspond to metabolic bur material.  Storage nitrogen is equated with the difference between maximum and critical nitrogen concentrations.  The values of each of these is specified as follows.

Minimum and critical are set to be equal to provide a configuration where Bur N is held in structural and storage pools only.  Storage N is parameterised therefore as the difference between minimum/critical N concentration and the following maximum N concentration.

```
{[Cotton].Bur.MinimumNConc}
{[Cotton].Bur.CriticalNConc}
{[Cotton].Bur.MaximumNConc}
```

**Senescence and Detachment**

Bur senescence can be specified to occur at differing rates before and after cutout.

```
{[Cotton].Bur.SenescenceRate}
```

where

Name | Description | Units
-|-|-
Constant	|Fraction of live bur that senesces on the current day | /day

**N reuse within the plant**

Non-structural N (ie storage or metabolic pools) can be available for reuse elsewhere within the plant to meet other demands via reallocation of N from senescing biomass or retranslocation from live biomass during some growth phases (e.g. reallocation of N from senescing bur or retranslocation from bur N storage to support daily growth.  The potential fraction of N that is available on any day is specified as follows:

```
{[Cotton].Bur.NRetranslocationFactor}
{[Cotton].Bur.NReallocationFactor}
```

from EMERGENCE:

During this time, the cotton plant exhibits rapid root growth. The primary root may be as much as 25-cm deep by the time the cotyledons unfold, and early season taproot growth proceeds at rates up to 6 cm per day under optimal
conditions (Oosterhuis, 1990; Ritchie et al., 2007; Snider and Oosterhuis, 2015).

CANOPY DEVELOPMENT:

Root growth also continues during early canopy and square development. In fact, the onset of flowering represents a shift in source-sink relations towards greater reproductive growth and a significant reduction in root growth. 

Thus, crop growth before flowering is critical for developing a well-established root system and sufficient canopy to support growth and yield.

Cotton root growth is rapid during the early part of the season and acts as the major sink for photosynthate until flowering and early boll development.

Children.Text:
Partitioning of daily growth into the various plant parts is calculated using partitioning fractions.  The sum of all partitioning fractions should equal one.  To ensure this, a simple staged approach is used here based on primary, secondary and (where required) tertiary partitioning.

1) partitioning to below and above ground growth is calculated.
2) Below ground growth is partitioned to the root model
3) Above ground growth is partitioned into reproductive material.  The remainder is partitioned to Vegetative material.
4) The above ground vegetative fraction is then partitioned to stem and leaf.  
5) The above ground reproductive fraction is then partitioned to bur, seed and lint.
5) The net result of all partitioning calculation should be a value of 1.
